Login: One Message for Two Failures

"No such user" and "wrong password" are different bugs, but the exact same response — on purpose.

// Figure 4.6: logging in (src/controllers/auth.controller.js, excerpt)
export const login = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body;
  const user = await userService.findUserByEmail(email);

  if (!user || !(await verifyPassword(password, user.password))) {
    throw new ApiError(401, 'Invalid email or password');
  }

  const token = signToken({ sub: user.id, role: user.role });
  const { password: _password, ...publicUser } = user;

  sendResource(res, { user: publicUser, token });
});

Two genuinely different problems collapse into the exact same if: !user (that email was never registered at all) and a user that exists but whose stored hash doesn't verifyPassword against the given password. It would be easy — and, from a purely logical standpoint, more precise — to tell those apart and return two different messages ("no account with that email" vs. "wrong password"). This project deliberately doesn't: separating them would let anyone probe /auth/login with a list of email addresses and learn, one response at a time, exactly which ones have an account here at all — information this API has no business handing out to an unauthenticated caller. One message, one status, regardless of which half failed.

findUserByEmail (unlike findUserById, previous topic) deliberately returns the full row, password hash included — the one place in this project that's correct, since this is the one comparison that genuinely needs it. It's why the destructure right after — const { password: _password, ...publicUser } = user — matters: without it, the hash would ride along into sendResource's response body, undoing the exact thing user.service.js's PUBLIC_FIELDS (register, previous slide) was careful to prevent everywhere else.
